To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a systematic assessment of difficult-to treat asthma can help to identify alternative or additional diagnosis, psychiatric illness or lack of compliance with therapy in a proportion of patients.

1) the diagnosis of asthma was incorrect in 20 of 100 patients referred to the tertiary centre with difficult-to-treat (step 4 and 5) asthma; 2) nonadherence with treatment, particularly with oral prednisolones, was more common in those with confirmed asthma; 3) 10 patients had a major psychiatric illness, which was not associated with the presence or absence of asthma.
1) the prevalence of difficult-to-tREAT asthma is 5%; and 2) the prevalence of noncompliance with prednisoLONE therapy is 50% in patients with difficult-to-TREAT asthma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of difficult-to-treatment asthma in adults.
a better understanding of the pathophysiology and management of asthma.
the evaluation and treatment of difficult-to-treate asthma, a group of patients who are often difficult to manage and who may have a number of different diagnoses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the diagnosis of asthma is confirmed in 70–75% of patients with “difficult-to-treat asthma”, whilst the remainder have alternative diagnoses, nonconcordance or psychiatric illness.

68% of patients with a diagnosis of difficult-to-treate asthma had asthma confirmed by demonstration of variable airflow limitation, 12% had alternative or additional diagnoses (mainly chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) and a further 12% had psychiatric problems or nonconcordant therapy.
the prevalence of difficult asthma is 5% of all asthmatics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
32% of patients with difficult-to-treat or intractable asthma have an alternative diagnosis, non-adherence to therapy or a psychiatric component.
difficult asthma is often due to noncompliance with therapy, misdiagnosis or psychiatric problems.
a substantial proportion of patients with difficult-to-treat or intractable asthma do not have asthma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a substantial proportion of difficult-to-treate asthmatic patients have a non-asthmatic condition.
the diagnosis of asthma should be confirmed by demonstration of airflow variability or reversibility in patients who are prescribed long-term oral glucorticoids.

a systematic approach to the diagnosis of difficult-to-tell asthma may be helpful to the clinician in identifying alternative or additional diagnoses in a substantial proportion (32% in our series) of cases, and may also identify a major psychiatric component in a substantial proportion.
